Nothing leaves the device while Veil is reconnecting.
Tor carries TCP only. Keep this on unless you know why you turned it off.
Lend your connection so people behind a firewall can reach Tor through your device. Only on Wi-Fi and while charging.
Android routes traffic through one VPN at a time. Grant the request to let Veil take it.
Which client the fronted transports look like. Modern filtering hashes this and asks whether the answer is plausible.
Snowflake carries data over WebRTC, whose own handshake has a fingerprint the setting above does not cover.
Any app on this device can reach these. They are open because tor needs them; the ports are randomised on every start.
Addresses that accepted a connection and then went silent. Retrying inside the penalty window achieves nothing and can make it longer.

Names ending in .ru, .рф, .su, .by or .kz are resolved and reached on the ordinary network. Banking apps and local sites start working again — and this network can see which of them you use. Off unless you turn it on.
Android throttles background apps after the screen has been off for a while, which shows up as a tunnel that is slow or dead when you come back to it. Exempting Veil keeps the connection alive.
Already exempt. The tunnel will not be suspended.
Straight to the Tor network. Fastest, and obvious to anyone watching the line.
Scrambles the stream so it matches no known protocol. Fast, but relies on bridge addresses that get discovered and blocked over time.
Looks like ordinary HTTPS to a site that really exists. The hardest to tell apart from normal browsing.
Hides inside traffic to a large CDN. Blocking it means blocking the CDN, which is expensive — but so is the latency you pay for it.
Hops through short-lived volunteer proxies found through a broker. No fixed address to block; needs UDP and a little patience.
Chosen once per installation, so no two devices look alike.
Common, current, and not the profile proxy software defaults to.
The most common browser, and for that reason the most imitated.
Chromium under another name; unremarkable on Windows networks.
Matches what this actually is: an app, not a browser. The profile is dated.
Matches no blocklist entry, and matches no real client either.
Looks like WebRTC from a real browser, which is what it is pretending to be.
A different browser each time: harder to blocklist, easier to notice.
The library\'s own handshake. Distinctive, and the fastest to set up.
Fastest. Everything you do shares an exit, so it can all be linked together.
The balance Tor Browser strikes: separate circuits per destination, so two sites cannot see each other\'s traffic as one user.
A new circuit for every connection. Hardest to correlate, and noticeably slower because each one has to be built.
Names are resolved at the exit relay. Nothing on your network sees what you look up.
DNS over TCP through the tunnel
Queries go to a public resolver as ordinary TCP, carried by the tunnel. Useful when a site behaves badly with exit-side resolution.
DNS over HTTPS through the tunnel
Queries go to a public resolver as HTTPS, carried by the tunnel. Same privacy from your network, and the resolver sees the tunnel rather than you.
Forget what worked on every network
Each one is a browser somewhere that could not reach Tor without help.

Built on the Tor Project\'s tor daemon, lyrebird and Snowflake, with a gVisor userspace network stack. Every component is free software, and nothing here needs an account or a server you have to find for yourself.
Every app on the device is routed through Veil. Pick one of the other two modes to make exceptions.
Bridges are unlisted entry points into Tor. Veil ships the public set, refreshes it from the Tor Project when it can, and can ask for private ones that no blocklist has yet.
This is the signature of a penalty rather than an outage: the connection was accepted and then quietly dropped.

No bridge address to block: the connection goes to a host that is not listening, and a router inside a cooperating network diverts it on the way past. Plain TCP, so carrier NAT does not affect it. Slow to start.

Tries every route until one reaches a relay, then measures what it built: round trip, throughput, name resolution and how steady it stays. Takes two to three minutes. Copy the result and send it back.
